summary: An April 1 joke RFC that defines a protocol for a Pi digit generation service between clients and servers. It is humorous and not a real standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This joke asks a computer to read out the digits of pi for you, one after another, which no one really needs.

subtitle: An April 1st joke proposing a network service to stream digits of pi on demand.

tldr.problem: Some computers lack local computing power to generate digits of pi, so they need a network service to provide them on demand.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3091 specifies PIgen, a protocol suite using TCP, UDP, and IP multicast services that stream digits of pi (and the approximation 22/7) from servers to clients on specific ports.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st joke RFC. The protocol is not intended for real use, though the RFC documents it in complete technical detail with service discovery and multiple transport options.

today: RFC 3091 is an April 1st humorous RFC published 1 April 2001. It was not intended as a serious protocol proposal and is clearly presented as humor.

sections.title: The PIgen Protocol Suite
sections.content:
RFC 3091 is an April 1st joke that proposes PIgen (Pi digit generation), a service where weak computers can ask powerful servers to stream the digits of pi. The essential trade-off, stated earnestly in the RFC, is the use of network resources and time instead of local computational cycles.

The protocol defines three services: a required TCP service on port 314159, an optional UDP service on port 314159, and an optional multicast service. The RFC even specifies DNS service discovery using SRV records and security considerations about trusting PIgen servers.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke proposes three different ways to ask a computer for the digits of pi: over a connection, one digit at a time in messages, or by listening to a radio broadcast.

sections.title: TCP and UDP Services
sections.content:
The TCP service is stateless. A client connects to port 314159, and the server streams one decimal digit of pi after the decimal point on each connection, starting with 1. The server discards any incoming data. Flow control is handled by TCP's normal mechanisms.

The UDP service is stateless and transactional. When a client sends a datagram requesting the nth digit of pi, the server responds with a datagram containing the value of that digit. An optional service on UDP port 220007 provides digits of the rational approximation 22/7 instead.
sections.plainLanguage: One way is like a phone line that streams digits forever. The other is like asking for a specific digit and getting just that one back.

sections.title: Multicast and Service Discovery
sections.content:
An optional IP multicast service sends a random distribution of pi digits to the multicast group 314.159.265.359. Clients assemble a coherent value of pi by listening over time. If no server is detected within 30 seconds, a client may become the provider.

Clients discover PIgen servers using DNS SRV records for the service "pigen" over tcp and udp. The approximate services use "pigem". The RFC notes the security consideration that the imminent collapse of the Internet is assured if clients do not use a trusted PIgen server, tongue firmly in cheek.
sections.plainLanguage: Another way is a radio broadcast sending random digits that listeners piece together over time. Computers find these services by asking DNS for the address.
